chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
title: Following Fats Waller around Harlem
summary: Whaley says that on arriving from Boston he followed Fats Waller, recalls him fleeing a process server over alimony, and 'Ain't Misbehavin'.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Yeah. And I used to follow him around just like I followed Fats Waller. When I first came to New York, all I did was follow Fats Waller.
Fats was playing at the Lafayette Theatre, and I came from Boston, and I had a great, long
overcoat, checkered --and I think I had a derby.
So before the phone rang, you were talking about Fats Waller, and you had this derby, and he had this long coat with the checks.
Yeah, and I had a pocketful of money and I used to hang around Fats and go into theatres and listen to him play and then go out somewhere, I'd be right with him, see.
And to me, Fats had more harmony in his fingers -- oh, he'd put that hand down and he would sing, and I followed Fats for a long while.

Yep. You know, he lives right by where we're sitting here doing this tape, is right down the street, one block down the street is where Fats Waller's home is, where he lived when he moved out here to Long Island.

Fats was at the theatre, see, and one day I was in there -- and Fats did a crecendo all the way down and he followed it on out the door. I said, 'Why are you running?' and he said, 'Well, didn't you see that man there?' and I said, 'What man?' and he said the man was coming to take him to jail because he didn't pay alimony.
But he was always in trouble about that kind of thing.
Oh yeah. He wrote -- wasn't it Fats who did 'Ain't Misbehavin'' -- $55 or $50 or something like that?
I think so -- $50 and a bottle of gin.
That's right. Then he wrote a lot of numbers.
